body.p: Claims 1-3, 5, 30, 37, 42, 43, 47, and 135-146 were previously pending in this application.

By this amendment, claim 1 has been amended to recite the limitations of claims 37 and 142. Accordingly, claims 37 and 142 have been cancelled without prejudice or disclaimer. In addition, claims 143-145 have been amended to maintain proper antecedent basis. No new matter has been added. In addition, it is believed that the amendments to claim 1, reciting the limitations of claims 37 and 142, do not alter the claims in such a way that a new search and examination would be warranted.
As a result, claims 1-3, 5, 30, 42, 43, 47, 135-141, and 143-146 are currently pending in this application for examination, with claim 1 being independent.

Claims 1-3, 5, 30, 37, 42, 43, 47, and 135-141 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Rylander, et al., U.S. Pat. Apl. Pub. No. 2013/0338627 ("Rylander") in view of Szunerits, et al., "Sensing using Localised Surface Plasmon Resonance Sensors," Chem. Comm., 2012, 48, 8999-9010 ("Szunerits"), and further in view of Hosokawa, et al., Nanoparticle Technology Handbook, 2007, pg. 365. The Patent Office alleges that Rylander generally teaches all features of claim 1 except for a particle attached to an end portion of a member, wherein the particle is positioned in an optically interrogatable position with respect to light transmitted through the member to the end portion. See pages 3-4 of the Office Action. The Patent Office further alleges that Szunerits teaches utilizing particles for surface plasmon resonance (SPR) and Hosokawa teaches attaching a particle to an optical fiber, and that it would have been obvious to combine Szunerits and Hosokawa with the device of Rylander. See pages 4-5 of the Office Action.

As an initial matter, it is submitted that the Patent Office has not acknowledged how or why one of ordinary skill in the art would have sought to attach a particle to the device taught in Rylander such that the particle is positioned in an optically interrogatable position with respect to light transmitted through the member to the end portion, as is recited in claim 1. The Patent Office alleges, for example, that it would have been obvious to combine Rylander with Szunerits because
Szunerits encourages increasing the aspect ratio of nanostructures results in higher sensitivities. See page 4 of the Office Action.

Rylander is generally directed to a minimally invasive fiber optic microneedle device that physically penetrates tissue for light-based therapeutics (see, for example, paragraph [0028] of Rylander). The device in Rylander is described as a light guiding microneedle that is used for therapy in human tissue (see, for example, paragraph [0161] of Rylander). In addition to delivering light, the microneedles may be used to deliver particulate nanomaterials (e.g., photoabsorbers) into tissue (see, for example, paragraphs [0283], [0295], and [0297] of Rylander). Paragraph [0309] of Rylander describes, for example, that photoabsorbers, such as single walled carbon nanohorns (SWNHs), may be dispended to a bladder using a hollow core fiber microneedle and syringe. Such nanomaterials, however, are not attached to the end portion of the member, as recited in independent claim 1.

Szunerits is generally directed to the fabrication of plasmonic nanosensors for SPR and linking nanostructures to surfaces, such as, for example, attaching gold nanostructures to a glass substrate (see the Abstract of Szunertis). It is not seen how or why the aspect ratio of a particle in Szunerits would be increased by attaching the particle to the device in Rylander. As would generally be understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art, an aspect ratio refers to an intrinsic property of a particle, e.g., the ratio of sizes of a particle in different dimensions. Attaching such a particle to a device would not have changed the aspect ratio of the particle, as suggested by the Patent Office. Therefore, there would have been no motivation to combine Rylander, which is directed to fiber optic microneedles for delivering light and/or photoabsorbers into tissue, with Szunerits, which is directed to the considerably different field of surface functionalization techniques for the fabrication of plasmonic nanosensors.

The Patent Office further alleges that it would have been obvious to combine Rylander with Hosokawa because Hosokawa encourages that attaching a particle to the end of an optical fiber can make the whole sensing system compact. See page 5 of the Office Action.
Rylander teaches that the described microneedles are difficult to insert into the skin, and thus, a support member for increasing the critical buckling force of the needle(s) to fortify the

needles for insertion into the skin is taught, for example, in paragraph [0228]. Rylander describes the microneedle may be embedded inside an elastic medium, such as a polymer (see, for example, paragraph [0216]). Other examples include a guidance ferrule template and an elastomeric support material for increasing the buckling force of the needle(s) (see, for example, paragraphs [0035] and [0155]). In addition, FIG. 1 of Rylander schematically shows that the microneedle is directly inserted into skin, and FIG. 4 of Rylander provides a series of photographic images of a microneedle inserted into skin.

Under such conditions, it is not seen how or why one of ordinary skill in the art would have had any motivation or rational reason to attach a particle onto the microneedle described in Rylander, or would have been able to do so with a reasonable expectation of success. Given such forces (which are described in detail in paragraphs [0217]-[0224] of Rylander), any such particle attached to the microneedle in Rylander would have been removed (e.g., "scraped off") from the microneedle as it was inserted into the skin, or other elastic medium. Thus, there would have been no rational or logical reason for adding a particle to the microneedle of Rylander. Instead, the reasonable expectation would have been that adding any such particles to the microneedle of Rylander would have been a futile exercise, since there would have been no way to prevent those particles from being removed from the microneedle, and therefore lost, as the microneedle is inserted into human skin.

In addition, with respect to Szunerits or Hosokawa, it is not seen where either of these would have overcome the deficiencies of Rylander in order to reach the claims. For instance, nowhere do either of Szunerits or Hosokawa teach or suggest attaching a particle to a microneedle in such a way as to keep it from becoming "scraped off' while the microneedle is inserted into the skin, as taught in Rylander. Both Szunerits and Hosokawa appear to be directed to detection techniques using metal particles, but neither of these references would have been useful in preventing particles attached to the microneedles from becoming lost as the microneedles were inserted into the skin as taught in Rylander. Thus, one of ordinary skill in the art would have been discouraged from making the proposed combination, as techniques for detecting particles on a microneedle are useless if the particles are no longer there.

The Patent Office states that the argument regarding there being no motivation to attach a particle onto the microneedle described in Rylander because the particle would be removed as the microneedle is inserted into skin is an intended use. See page 8 of the Office Action. It is submitted that the purpose of Rylander is provide light delivering microneedles that reduce pain associated with insertion of the microneedles into living tissue (see, for example, paragraph [0016] of Rylander). If the microneedle described in Rylander were modified with a particle as suggested by the Patent Office, a person of ordinary skill in the art would have recognized that the particle would be removed from the microneedle as it was inserted into skin, because, as described by Rylander, the microneedles require an increased buckling strength to penetrate skin (see, for example, paragraph [0238] of Rylander). It is therefore submitted that one of ordinary skill in the art, in view of the teachings of Rylander, Szunerits, and Hosokawa, would not have been motivated or found any rational reason to have attached a particle in an optically interrogatable position on the device in Rylander for the reasons outlined above.

Furthermore, without conceding to the merits of the rejection and to expedite prosecution, independent claim 1 has been amended to recite the features of dependent claims 37 and 142, i.e., the at least one particle is at least partially coated with a reaction entity comprising a binding partner to which an analyte binds.

Regarding claim 37, the Patent Office alleges that paragraph [0306] of Rylander teaches a particle coated with a reaction entity. See page 5 of the Office Action. Paragraph [0306] of Rylander, however, merely describes the investigation of the efficacy of SWNHs as exogenous chromophores. Nowhere does Rylander teach or suggest that the particles (e.g., SWNHs) are coated with a reaction entity, as alleged by the Patent Office.
Regarding claim 142, as summarized below, the Patent Office alleges that Goncalves

teaches a reaction entity comprising a binding partner to which an analyte binds because Goncalves describes hydrogel nanoparticles that are capable of including small molecular weight molecules. The Patent Office states that it would have been obvious to use the nanoparticles of Goncalves within the device of Rylander, Szunerits, and Hosokawa to afford a device for the delivery of bioactive molecules capable of the detection of a variety of analytes. See page 6 of the Office

Action. Goncalves, however, is generally directed to self-assembled polymeric nanogels for drug delivery applications (see the Abstract of Goncalves). Nowhere does Goncalves teach or suggest that a particle coated with a reaction entity comprises a binding partner to which an analyte binds. Instead, Goncalves describes that hydrogel particles may be used as drug delivery systems for cell targeting and controlled and sustained drug release at the target site. See, for example, pages 1428- 1431 in conjunction with Table 1. It is submitted that drug delivery using a hydrogel as the delivery platform, as taught by Goncalves, neither teaches nor suggests a nanoparticle comprising a coating that includes a reaction entity to which an analyte binds, as recited in amended independent claim 1.

For at least the reasons outlined above, the combination of Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa (and Goncalves) does not render amended independent claim 1 obvious, and claim 1 is patentable over the combination of Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa (and Goncalves). The remaining claims that stand rejected on this ground depend from independent claim 1, and are therefore also patentable over the combination of Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa (and Goncalves) for at least the reasons outlined above. In addition, it is not conceded that Rylander, Szunerits, or Hosokawa (and Goncalves), alone or in combination, teach or render obvious any of the features recited in claims claims 1-3, 5, 30, 37, 42, 43, 47, and 135-141, as asserted by the Patent Office.
Claims 142, 143, 145, and 146 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being

unpatentable over Rylander in view of Szunerits and Hosokawa and further in view of Goncalves et al., "Self-Assembled Hydrogel Nanoparticles for Drug Delivery Applications," Materials, 2010, 3(2), 1420-1460.

Independent claim 1 has been amended to recite the dependent features of claim 142, which is patentable over the combination of Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa, and Goncalves for at least the reasons outlined above.

Claims 143, 145, and 146 depend from claim 1, which is patentable over Rylander, Szunerits, and Hosokawa for at least the reasons outlined above. Goncalves fails to cure the deficiencies of Rylander, Szunerits, and Hosokawa noted above with respect to independent claim

1. Accordingly, claims 143, 145, and 146 are also patentable over the combination of Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa, and Goncalves. In addition, it is not conceded that Goncalves teaches any of the features recited in claims 143, 145, or 146, and it is not conceded that it would have been obvious to combine Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa, and Goncalves in the manner suggested in the Office Action. Withdrawal of the claim rejections on this ground is respectfully requested.

Claim 144 stands rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Rylander in view of Szunerits and Hosokawa and further in view of Gautum et al., "Adsorption kinetics of ammonia sensing by graphene films decorated with platinum nanoparticles," Journal of Applied Physics, 2012, 111, 094317.
Claim 144 depends from claim 1, which is patentable over Rylander, Szunerits, and

Hosokawa for at least the reasons outlined above. Gautam fails to cure the deficiencies of Rylander, Szunerits, and Hosokawa noted above with respect to independent claim 1. Accordingly, claim 144 is also patentable over the combination of Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa, and Gautam. In addition, it is not conceded that Gautam teaches any of the features recited in claim 144, and it is not conceded that it would have been obvious to combine Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa, and Gautam in the manner suggested in the Office Action. Withdrawal of the claim rejections on this ground is respectfully requested.

In view of the foregoing, this application should now be in condition for allowance. A notice to this effect is respectfully requested. If the Examiner believes, after this response, the application is not in condition for allowance, the Examiner is requested to call the undersigned at the telephone number indicated below to discuss any outstanding issues.
No fee is believed due with this Amendment. However, if a fee is due with this
